title: In-memory cache
purpose: Measure key-value throughput against a Valkey instance this agent creates in a container and destroys when the module ends - never against a cache already on this machine.

implementation.note: The server and both measurement tools come from the pinned image, run through container::Sandbox::exec with fixed argument vectors. No RESP client exists in this workspace and nothing on the host is involved.

dependencies: A container runtime (Docker or Podman) whose daemon is reachable
1 GiB of free memory, which is the sandbox's ceiling rather than what this workload uses
max_network_bytes_note: The Valkey image, once, on a machine that does not already have it. The fetch is explicit and happens before anything is timed; nothing crosses the network during the measurement itself.

safety.target: a Valkey container this module starts, published on 127.0.0.1 on a port the runtime assigns
never: a cache already running on this machine
an operator-supplied host, port or socket
an image that is not pinned to a digest
safety.note: docs/THREAT-MODEL.md (T-DB) applies here exactly as it does to database.oltp: the module creates and destroys its own instance or reports itself not measured. There is no fallback to a server on the host and no configuration that could introduce one.

sandbox.user: 999:1000, the image's own valkey account. The uid and gid differ, which is why the allow-list carries a pair per image rather than one number reused.
sandbox.capabilities: all dropped, no-new-privileges set, no host path mounted, no device passed
sandbox.data_directory: /data on a 512 MiB tmpfs owned by the service account, mode 0700
sandbox.memory: 1 GiB, the isolation tier's ceiling rather than this workload's need
sandbox.readiness: redis-cli -h 127.0.0.1 ping, run inside the container. It exits 1 on a refused connection, which is what makes it a probe rather than a command that runs.
sandbox.lifetime: removed when the module returns, on every path including failure. Anything a killed run leaves behind carries this agent's label and is reaped at the start of the next one.

preparation: None. The server starts empty and redis-benchmark populates the key space as it measures, which is the workload rather than a setup step.
calibration: Fixed request counts rather than a duration target, because redis-benchmark reports a rate over a request count and a duration-calibrated run would measure a different number of keys on every machine.
warmup: None. Each shape's first requests populate the key space it then reads, and the rate reported is over the whole command; on a 10,000-key space at 100,000 requests the populating fraction is small and identical on every machine.

workloads.description: GET across a 10,000-key space, 50 clients, 64-byte values
workloads.represents: The read a cache exists to serve - a page fragment, a session, a query result

workloads.description: SET over the same space and value size
workloads.represents: Populating the cache, and every write-through
Counters and rate limiters: the shape an application cannot do client-side without a race
What the machine does once the per-command round trip is amortised away - the difference between `buy a faster machine` and `batch your calls`

workloads.description: Mean round trip on an otherwise idle server
workloads.represents: The floor under every cache hit, paid once per call however fast the server is

workloads.description: The worst round trip observed while idle
workloads.represents: Scheduler and allocator jitter - one observation, not a distribution

repetitions.note: Fixed at 100,000 requests per command regardless of profile, for the same reason database.oltp fixes its phase duration: a profile-dependent request count would make two runs of the same machine incomparable.

validation: A command that reported no operations per second is withheld rather than published as a zero, which would read as a server that could not perform it at all.
The unloaded round-trip probe is withheld unless it collected samples; a mean of zero from a parse that found nothing would read as an extraordinarily fast machine.
An image that is not pinned to a digest is not run at all.
abort_conditions: no container runtime, or a runtime whose daemon does not answer
the container exits during startup, in which case its own log is reported
cleanup: The container is removed when the module ends, including on failure. Anything a crashed run leaves behind carries this agent's label and is removed at the start of the next run.
limitations: There is no latency-under-load metric. redis-benchmark is closed-loop and has no rate limiter, so its p50/p95/p99 columns are percentiles of an experiment where offered load fell whenever the server slowed. They are parsed by nothing here and published nowhere.
`roundtrip.unloaded_*` is measured on an otherwise idle server. It is a floor under every cache hit, not a distribution, and the metric key says `unloaded` so it cannot be read as one.
redis-benchmark shares the container with the server, so its CPU is CPU the server did not get. Every figure here is a floor.
The data directory is a tmpfs. An RDB snapshot is still written, but to RAM, so these figures describe the server and the CPU rather than the disk.

Valkey serves commands from a single thread, so these figures track per-core speed and barely move with core count. What core count does change is whether the benchmark client starves the server, which is why a figure from a two-core machine is a floor twice over.
Each metric is one command and one figure, so no coefficient of variation is computed and stability_cv_bound is not enforced against these.

scoring.note: GET carries the most weight because it is what a cache is for. The unloaded round trip is next because an application that reaches its cache twenty times to build a page pays it twenty times, and no amount of throughput headroom reduces it. The maximum round trip carries the least: it is a single observation, and a single outlier is exactly what it is made of. Reference anchors are declared targets, not measurements.
